summary: Victoria Song, a self-described smart glasses skeptic, reviews the $299 Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses for The Verge and finds them the most practical smart glasses she has worn. They improve on camera, audio, call quality, style options, and the charging case, though the AI features are limited or not yet available and battery life could be better. She also raises privacy questions about the LED indicator and filming in public, concluding that Meta nailed the execution rather than reinventing smart glasses.
one_line: The Verge's review finds the $299 Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses stylish and well executed, with good camera and audio, but limited AI and unresolved privacy concerns.
key_facts: The Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses cost $299 and received a Verge Score of 7.
They come in 150 style variations across two frame styles, seven colors, and multiple lens options including color, prescription, and transitions.
The camera was upgraded from 5MP to 12MP, with photos at 3024 x 4032 pixels and videos at 1080p at 30 frames per second.
The glasses now have five mics instead of one, including one in the nose pad, which makes calls sound clear.
Videos max out at one minute, and all photos and videos are vertical with no landscape option.
Battery life is five to six hours on light use and three to four hours with heavy photo and video use; a 70-minute commute as headphones drained about 18 to 20 percent.
The slimmer USB-C charging case has an LED button that turns orange while charging and green when full; one test went from 15 percent to 100 percent in under an hour.
Importing 143 photos and videos over the glasses' local Wi-Fi with the Meta View app took about five minutes.
Livestreaming works only with Facebook and Instagram, which Song calls a limitation that echoes why Snap's Spectacles never took off.
The Meta voice assistant sounds natural but is slow and can't do much yet; the feature to identify objects through the camera is not available yet.

Meta made the LED capture light impossible to disable and gave it a pulsing pattern, but Song's co-workers and friends gave mixed reports on whether it is noticeable, and no one noticed her filming in public.
Transition lenses cost $80 more, and prescriptions from Ray-Ban or LensCrafters cover the -6 to +4 range; ordering elsewhere voids the warranty.
Song says Meta's glasses are not revolutionary but a turning point, appealing most to gadget nerds and content creators.
